title: A mind without fear
hookLine: a sage tells a king he has reached fearlessness, and a poet asks the same for a whole people
carry: abhaya: the raised palm says fear not
tomorrow: Arjuna asks, why act at all?

cards: A king sits with a sage. The king is Janaka, ruler of Videha. The sage is Yajnavalkya.

In the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, Yajnavalkya asks the king where he'll go when he leaves this body, and the king admits he doesn't know. So the sage teaches him the Self: not this, not that, never grasped, never harmed.
And at the end he says: Janaka, you have reached fearlessness. The king's answer is to wish the same gift back on his teacher, and to place his kingdom at the sage's service.

teach.b: That word is abhaya, fearlessness, and it runs all through Hindu teaching. Another Upanishad, the Taittiriya, says that one who knows the bliss of Brahman fears nothing at all.

Teachers often explain it this way: fear grips the small self that thinks it can be lost; knowing the deeper Self, which can't be harmed, loosens the grip. You can see the teaching in almost any temple.
Look at the raised right hand on an image of Ganesha, or Lakshmi, or the dancing Shiva: palm open, fingers up, facing you. That's the abhaya mudra, the gesture that means fear not. Now Tagore.

teach.h: WHERE THE MIND IS WITHOUT FEAR.
teach.b: In one Gitanjali poem he stacks one small word, where, line on line: "Where the mind is without fear and the head is held high; Where knowledge is free; Where the world has not been broken up into fragments by narrow domestic walls."

teach.h: MY FATHER, LET MY COUNTRY AWAKE.
teach.b: Then it lands as a prayer: "Into that heaven of freedom, my Father, let my country awake." Readers hear it about a nation waking, or about one person.
Either way, it asks God for the gift Yajnavalkya named: a mind without fear. And here's where it meets your week. Before a test, a hard talk, a first day, the Hindu answer isn't just be brave.
Many teachers put it this way: the deepest you, the Self, is not the thing at risk.

how: Many Hindu images show the abhaya mudra, the raised open palm that means fear not; Tagore's 'Where the mind is without fear' is a poem some readers learn by heart and recite at school or at gatherings about freedom.

games.q: an image of Ganesha holds up his right palm, open, facing you. what is he saying?
games.why: it's the abhaya mudra: fear not. the same fearlessness Yajnavalkya named for King Janaka, and Tagore asked God for in his poem.

practice: This is darshan, the Hindu practice of seeing God and being seen. Find an image with a raised palm, Ganesha, Lakshmi, the dancing Shiva, on a family altar, a phone, or in your mind.

Sit with the head held high, chin level, neck long, without strain. Look at the open palm facing you. Name one fear sitting in you today, a test, a hard conversation, a phone call, and hear the gesture answer it: fear not.
If you pray, end with Tagore's own line, into that heaven of freedom, my Father, let my country awake; if you don't, rest your eyes on the palm and notice what in you is still steady.

wordCard.voice: Tagore's Gitanjali. A prayer for a mind without fear: the gift the Upanishad calls abhaya, and every temple shows in a raised palm.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: abhaya, fearlessness, literally 'no fear'. The word Yajnavalkya says to Janaka.

carryVoice: Your line: abhaya: the raised palm says fear not. That's three days with Tagore. Tomorrow, Arjuna asks why he should act at all.
